clinician.final_diagnosis: cblC deficiency associated with anti-factor H antibody-associated hemolytic uremic syndrome
clinician.trajectory_summary: A 19-year-old woman presented with acute kidney failure and severe neurologic impairment, asthenia, dyspnea, hypertension, and lower limb edema. Initial laboratory tests revealed acute kidney injury, anemia, and evidence of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (elevated LDH, low haptoglobin, schistocytes). Further investigation showed elevated serum homocysteine, normal vitamin B12 and folate, low plasma and urinary methionine, and high methylmalonic aciduria, strongly suggesting cblC deficiency. Anti-factor H antibody testing was positive. Genetic testing confirmed cblC deficiency with two pathogenic variants in the MMACHC gene.

key_supporting_evidence.claim: Patient presented with acute kidney failure and severe neurologic impairment, asthenia, dyspnea, high blood pressure, and lower limb edema.

Initial labs showed acute kidney injury (creatinine 246 μmol/L), anemia (hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL), and evidence of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (LDH 700 U/L, haptoglobin < 0.08 g/L, schistocytes on peripheral blood smear).
Proteinuria (7.6 g/g of creatinine) and hematuria (348.103/mL) were present.
Serum homocysteine was significantly increased (285 μmol/L), with normal vitamin B12 and folate levels.
Plasma and urinary amino acid chromatography indicated low levels of methionine (12 μmol/L and < 1 respectively).
High levels of methylmalonic aciduria (247 mmol/mol of creatinine) were detected.
Antibody testing for complement factor H (CFH) was positive (7450 UA/ml).
Genetic sequencing of the MMACHC gene showed two heterozygous pathogenic variants (c.556G > A and c.271dupA), confirming cblC deficiency.

ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.basis: Serum levels of vitamin B12 and folate were normal (E006).
